source_read: In-press PDF (Drug and Alcohol Dependence, article in press, DAD-4597), PDF pp. 1–8 (all pages); text layer used for searching; every number used checked on pages rendered at 150 dpi (Tables 1–4 on PDF pp. 3–5, Methods PDF p. 2, Discussion PDF p. 6). Cited as 'PDF p. N of the in-press version'.

claims.overstatement: None in the part of the claim that comes from this source: the claim gives the restriction to people with the disorder, the recalled ages, the lack of age adjustment, the size of the difference and the authors' own reading. One count is stated loosely (see note).
claims.note: Checked against this source: NESARC 2001–2002, 43,093 adults interviewed once face to face, response 81% (PDF p. 2); comparison restricted to 2,080 men and 1,217 women (3,297) with lifetime DSM-IV cannabis abuse, dependence or both (PDF pp. 1–2); weighted means (SE) men vs women, first use 16.71 (0.10) vs 16.73 (0.12), p 0.8768; onset 19.34 (0.13) vs 18.98 (0.16), F 2.73, p 0.1035; time from first use to onset 2.64 (0.10) vs 2.24 (0.13), F 5.20, p 0.0259 (Table 3, PDF p. 4); difference 0.40 years = 4.8 months; editors' approximate 95% CI reproduced from the two SEs as 0.079 to 0.721 (an interval matching the printed Wald F, implied SE 0.175, would be slightly wider, about 0.06 to 0.74; both approximate); no adjustment for current age or anything else in these comparisons (PDF p. 2, 2.3), while women with the disorder were younger (Table 1, PDF p. 3); 11.8% vs 5.4% lifetime prevalence cited from Stinson et al. (2006) (PDF pp. 1–2); the authors call the 0.40 years evidence of telescoping (PDF pp. 1, 3, 6) in a general-population sample in which only 14.20% of men and 12.43% of women had sought any treatment (Table 4, PDF p. 5). The paper nowhere reports a 2.5-year difference, and its sample is 3,297 people in all (1,217 women, 2,080 men), so a description as '1,217 women and 3,297 men' with a 2.5-year gap does not match it. Loose count: 'one of about 50 comparisons' counts outcomes (30 comorbidity rows, 12 course rows, 10 help-seeking rows = 52); the number of tests made without correction is larger (each comorbidity row has two odds ratios, so about 82 in Tables 2–4, and about 103 with the 21 category contrasts of Table 1). Suggest 'more than 50 comparisons' or 'about 50 outcomes'. The disorder's onset is not defined further (first abuse or dependence), and how many had dependence rather than abuse only is not reported, so the endpoint is 'cannabis use disorder', as the claim says, not dependence. No dosing or advice content.

anchors.page: PDF p. 2 of the in-press version
anchors.extracted: NESARC 2001–2002: US civilian non-institutionalized adults aged 18 and over in households and group quarters; face-to-face interviews with 43,093 by Census Bureau interviewers; response rate 81%; Black, Hispanic and young adults oversampled, data weighted for oversampling, non-response and to the 2000 census. Study sample: 2,080 men and 1,217 women with lifetime cannabis abuse, dependence or both.

anchors.page: PDF p. 2 of the in-press version
anchors.extracted: AUDADIS-IV DSM-IV cannabis abuse and dependence criteria. Course measures: ages at first use, heavy use (daily or more than 20 days a month), onset of the disorder and remission, all reported at the interview; telescoping measured as time from age at first use to age at onset of the disorder.

anchors.page: PDF p. 2 of the in-press version
anchors.extracted: Gender differences in clinical course computed as weighted means with design-based SEs (SUDAAN); covariate adjustment only in the comorbidity logistic models; differences judged by 95% CIs excluding 1, with no correction for multiple comparisons.

anchors.page: PDF p. 4 of the in-press version
anchors.extracted: Men (n 2,080) vs women (n 1,217), weighted mean (SE): age at first use 16.71 (0.10) vs 16.73 (0.12), Wald F 0.02, p 0.8768; age at heavy use 18.15 (0.16) vs 18.28 (0.25), p 0.6676; age at onset 19.34 (0.13) vs 18.98 (0.16), F 2.73, p 0.1035; time from first use to onset 2.64 (0.10) vs 2.24 (0.13) years, F 5.20, p 0.0259. Difference 0.40 years, about 5 months; approximate 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72 from the two SEs (my calculation, ignoring covariance).

anchors.page: PDF p. 3 of the in-press version
anchors.locator: 3. Results › 3.3 Clinical characteristics and course of lifetime cannabis use disorder, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: No gender difference in age at first or heavy use or at onset; the interval from first use to onset was longer in men (2.64 vs 2.24 years, F = 5.20, p < .05), which the authors take as evidence for telescoping in cannabis use disorder.

anchors.page: PDF p. 3 of the in-press version
anchors.extracted: Women with the disorder were younger: aged 18–29, 35.82% of women vs 29.19% of men; over 45, 21.13% vs 28.66% (OR for men 1.66, 95% CI 1.34–2.06); current age not adjusted for in the Table 3 comparisons.

anchors.page: PDF pp. 1–2 of the in-press version
anchors.locator: 1. Introduction, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 1); 3. Results › 3.1 Sociodemographic characteristics, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2)
anchors.extracted: Lifetime cannabis use disorder in 11.8% of men and 5.4% of women, cited from an earlier NESARC analysis (Stinson et al., 2006, Psychol. Med.), not computed in this paper.

anchors.page: PDF p. 5 of the in-press version
anchors.extracted: Ever sought any treatment: 14.20% (SE 0.98) of men vs 12.43% (1.03) of women with the disorder (OR 1.17, 0.92–1.48): a mostly untreated general-population sample.

anchors.page: PDF pp. 1, 6 of the in-press version
anchors.extracted: Abstract: women experienced telescoping to the disorder. Discussion: shorter interval in women despite no differences in ages, said to accord with clinical and community studies; the authors add that their group's general-population alcohol analysis (Keyes et al., 2010) suggests telescoping may not occur in general-population samples and that telescoping may be sample- and substance-specific; closing paragraph restates evidence for telescoping among women.

anchors.page: PDF p. 6 of the in-press version
anchors.extracted: Limitations named by the authors: self-report not confirmed by collateral informants; cross-sectional design; household survey may miss people with the disorder (shelters and group homes sampled). Recall of ages and lack of age adjustment not named.

key_findings.note: CI reproduced from the SEs (0.079–0.721); an interval consistent with the printed Wald F (implied SE about 0.175) would be slightly wider, about 0.06 to 0.74. Either is approximate.
Arithmetic reproduced: crude within-disorder ORs 1.343, 1.929, 1.595 vs main × interaction 1.35, 1.943, 1.585; also SUD 1.557 vs 1.548 and any mood 0.450 vs 0.456; z for 95.57 vs 94.14 = 1.43.

reporting_issues.note: Among the disorders named, women with the disorder had the higher percentage only for nicotine dependence, bipolar I and II and conduct disorder.
Reproduced: non-seekers about 1,785 men and 1,066 women; p(1−p)/SE² gives 97 to 182 effective respondents per row (help-seeking rows about 1,030 to 1,270).
Reference list title (PDF p. 7): transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine (Drug Alcohol Depend. 115).

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, overall moderate: right for the weighted descriptions; the analytic telescoping statement is weaker, as the reasoning says.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One detail: 'among about 50 comparisons' (gap 3) and the outcomes field's '52 outcomes ... besides 11 sociodemographic characteristics' count outcomes, not tests: Tables 2–4 hold about 82 tests (two odds ratios per comorbidity row) and Table 1 compares 10 characteristics with 21 category contrasts (11 is the Methods list including gender).

missed: PDF p. 2, 2.2 Measures, 4th paragraph: 'onset of CUD' is not defined (first abuse or first dependence criterion set), and with abuse-only cases included the interval may end at a cannabis abuse diagnosis; worth stating in the operationalization alongside the unreported abuse/dependence split already noted.

Table 3 p-values fit a Wald F with about 65 design degrees of freedom (F 5.20 → p 0.0259); not an error, but it explains why an interval from the printed SEs is a little narrower than one from the printed F.
